Universal Coloring

Graph TheoryCountingAlgorithms
Game: Put colours round a circle so that every pair of colours shows up next to each other somewhere as you go round.
How to play: Click a dot to change its colour, and choose how many colours to use. Tick Show pairs to see which pairs you have made.

From the row colour to the column colour: a filled dot means you have made that pair.

Show on dots
Look for the math

With four colours there are sixteen ordered pairs of colours. The circle has sixteen dots, so it also has sixteen neighbour pairs. Can every possible pair be there at once? A circle like this is called a de Bruijn sequence.

Count the gaps

With n colours and n² dots there are exactly n² gaps between neighbouring dots, counting the gap from the last dot back to the first. There are also exactly n² ordered pairs of colours. So if all the pairs appear, each one appears exactly once. There is no room for a repeat. The logic test checked this for every colouring of 4 and 9 dots.

Turn pairs into arrows

Make a directed graph with one vertex for each colour. Draw an arrow from a to b whenever pair a,b occurs. Every arrow is present, including the loops from a colour to itself. Each vertex therefore has n arrows leaving and n arriving. Going round the circle is a closed walk that uses every arrow once: an Euler cycle. Reading the circle the other way just reverses every arrow, so the pairs are all there in that direction too.

A walk that always finishes

Because incoming and outgoing arrows balance, you can build the cycle by taking unused arrows from any starting colour and splicing in small closed loops when you come back early. That is Hierholzer's method. The applet page says there is "no way to get stuck"; taken literally that is not quite right. With two colours, the greedy walk 0,0,1,0 stops back at 0 after three of the four arrows, missing 1,1. What is true is that you can always splice that short loop in and finish. The test built the cycle from every starting colour for 2 to 6 colours and checked all n² pairs in both directions.

What the test checked

For 2 and 3 colours it tried all 2⁴ = 16 and 3⁷ = 19,683 colourings and compared its pair chart and its colour-changing move with a second, independent reading of the applet's own methods. For 4, 5 and 6 colours, where listing every colouring is impossible, it checked the constructed cycles and thousands of other colourings. It also confirmed that n² − 1 dots can never hold all n² pairs.

Set two colours and find a circle yourself. Then read it backwards: did you need to start again?
